title: 4 Ideas on How to Teach in a Time of Curriculum Battles
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler argues that teachers anxious about state laws restricting certain concepts should still teach history and other politically sensitive content, and offers four ideas. First, know the law: the statutes bar teaching that students should feel guilt, not teaching events that make them uncomfortable. Second, know your audience, since actual complaints are often fewer than feared and opt-outs are better than district-wide vetoes. Third, distinguish settled from open questions and avoid presenting contested interpretations as the truth. Fourth, prepare students with facts and perspectives before discussion, as in the Four-Question Method. The common thread is that students must not be left ignorant of important events because of vague fear of complaints.
points: Teaching about uncomfortable events is not the same as teaching that students should feel uncomfortable, and the laws only target the latter.
Fear of the laws can exceed the real threat, and parent opt-outs are a better response than district-wide vetoes.
Teachers should separate settled facts from contested perspectives and avoid presenting their own views as the truth.
Students should learn the facts and each side's perspective before debating, starting with less charged issues.
quotes: Not surprisingly, some teachers say they’re steering clear of any content that might trigger a complaint. But that could leave students in the dark about important events—especially in history, an area where students’ knowledge is, on average, already seriously lacking.
But the laws don’t prohibit teaching about events that make kids uncomfortable. They prohibit teaching that students should feel uncomfortable.
In many classrooms, teachers’ fears about the laws, or parental complaints generally, may be out of proportion to the actual threat.

In that case, it makes sense to enable parents to opt their children out of reading materials they find objectionable. That’s not ideal, but it’s better than giving them the power to veto a text or even a curriculum across an entire district.
Teachers don’t need to lie. They don’t need to exclude factual information about the darker side of American history, and they don’t need to stifle discussion.

Ideally, students will first have a good grasp of the facts and the perspectives of those on each side of an issue before offering their own views. It also helps to start with issues that are less likely to tap into strong pre-existing beliefs.

Most members of the public agree that legislators shouldn’t try to control what gets taught in the classroom. And clearly, these laws are making a tough job a lot harder. Nevertheless, teachers owe it to their students—and to all of us—to find a way to convey the information and knowledge essential for informed participation in a democracy.
